sources.supported_claim: Compare market contracting with the costs of organizing transactions inside a firm; expansion is limited by internal organizing costs and allocation errors. Technology can change internal and market costs differently.
sources.limits: A comparative theoretical argument, not a measured DAMS cost advantage. Coase explicitly discusses internal costs. Fixed-organization scale tests do not estimate efficient firm boundaries or effects on firm size.

additional_reading.visual_inspection_scope: Only listed figure/table/formula or image-only pages have been visually inspected; this is not an all-pages visual-layout audit.
claim_reassessment: Coase explicitly analyzes internal organizing costs, error losses and heterogeneous transactions; an internal-governance gap cannot be defined as his omission of all internal costs.
1937 pp394–397 compare marginal internal organization with market/another entrepreneur; technology changes both cost curves, so improved management need not universally enlarge firms.
Firm boundary and legal employment/control relation differ; governance shares alone do not replace contractual authority.

sources.checked_locator: pp. 1–2; p. 12 footnote 12; p. 23 divided authority discussion
sources.supported_claim: The right to decide differs from effective control, which depends on information acquisition and organizational conditions. Initiative effects depend on congruence and consent; delegation or divided authority can reduce initiative in the described countercases.
sources.limits: Formal theory under specific information and incentive assumptions. It neither identifies DAMS influence numerically nor supplies signal-noise coefficients. Common-value voting omits private project benefits, strategic information acquisition and veto conflict; a reversed effort coefficient does not represent these mechanisms.

claim_reassessment: Initiative advantage depends on the assumed reaction curves and congruence; footnote 12 p12 gives an outside-project counterexample in which delegation reduces initiative.
Formal versus real authority is not a recommendation for continuous voting weights; text permits authority allocated across many decisions and contingent delegation.
Splitting authority may enhance or reduce initiative depending on congruence and veto/majority arrangements; formal shares are not observed real authority.

claim_reassessment: Verification of encoded propositions and robustness is explicitly different from theory contribution; new insight must arise through experimentation or failed verification.
Validation is empirical comparison, especially important if starting theory is nonempirical; synthetic parameter ranges or matched worlds cannot substitute for it.
Time horizon and replicates require justification; intervals address sampling uncertainty conditional on the model, not behavioral calibration.
